title: The road to Emmaus (Luke 24:13–35)
hook: two sad friends walk seven miles with a stranger and know him in the breaking of bread

segments.voice: Yesterday, Mary Magdalene in the garden: she took him for the gardener until he said her name. Your line was he says your name. Whose name did you say like it mattered? Day sixty-nine.

Same Sunday, late afternoon. Two of Jesus's followers are walking home from Jerusalem to a village called Emmaus, about seven miles away. One is named Cleophas. The other, Luke never names. They're going over it again and again, the way you do after a funeral, on the long drive home. A stranger falls into step beside them and asks what they're talking about. They stop. Their faces fall. Are you the only visitor in Jerusalem who hasn't heard? And then the saddest words in the chapter: we had hoped he was the one. Had hoped. Past tense. Today: the longest walk of Easter day.
screen: `SEVEN MILES, WALKING HOME.` → `A STRANGER FALLS INTO STEP.` → `WE HAD HOPED.`

segments.voice: The stranger is Jesus, but Luke says their eyes were held so they didn't know him. And he doesn't reveal himself. He walks with them and opens the Scriptures, from Moses through all the prophets, showing how the Messiah had to suffer and so enter his glory. Seven miles of Bible study. At the village he acts as if he's going further. And they beg him, in the Douay-Rheims: "Stay with us, because it is towards evening, and the day is now far spent." He goes in. At the table he takes the bread, blesses it, breaks it and gives it to them. The same four movements as the Last Supper. And their eyes are opened, they know him, and he vanishes. Then they turn to each other: "Was not our heart burning within us, whilst he spoke in the way, and opened to us the scriptures?" It's dark, and they walk the seven miles back anyway, to tell the others how they knew him "in the breaking of bread." Catholics see the shape of every Mass in this road. First the Word: the Scriptures read and opened. Then the table: bread taken, blessed, broken, given. Two parts, the same order Luke tells it. And notice where he's recognized. Not in the explaining, as good as it was. In the bread. Pope John Paul II named a letter on the Eucharist after the disciples' plea, stay with us, Lord.
screen: `THEIR EYES WERE HELD.` · `SEVEN MILES OF SCRIPTURE.` · `TOOK, BLESSED, BROKE, GAVE.` · `THE WORD, THEN THE TABLE: THE MASS.` · then, large: `WAS NOT OUR HEART BURNING WITHIN US?`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: walk with someone who is sad. Settle and breathe. Bring to mind someone whose hope has gone into the past tense lately: we had hoped, I used to think. Picture yourself falling into step beside them. You don't need the right words. The stranger started with a question and let them talk. Think of one question you could ask them this week, and then just listen. If you pray, you can ask to be good company on someone's road. The bell holds the time.
The road to Emmaus. Two sad friends, seven miles, a stranger who opened the Scriptures, and bread broken at the end of the day. Today's word.
Your line: was not our heart burning. Tonight, look back over the day and notice one moment that warmed you, even if you didn't see it at the time. Day sixty-nine.

howItsDone: Catholics often hear the Emmaus story during the Easter season, and many see in it the two parts of every Mass: the Liturgy of the Word and the Liturgy of the Eucharist.

original.note: Greek: the breaking of the bread, one of the earliest Christian names for the Eucharist.

trapdoor: what you thought: a story about a walk.
what it means: two people who've lost hope are met on the road, have the Scriptures opened, and recognize him at the table.
what a scholar hears: took, blessed, broke, gave: the Last Supper's four verbs. the Word, then the bread, the shape Catholics find in every Mass. and nobody is sure where Emmaus was.

notes: Douay-Rheims wording of Luke 24:29, 24:32 and 24:35 given from memory; confirm (e.g. 'whilst' and 'the scriptures' lowercase).
Distance: the Douay-Rheims says 'sixty furlongs'; about seven miles. Some manuscripts read 160 furlongs. The location of Emmaus is uncertain (several sites claimed).
CCC 1347 draws the Emmaus parallel to the Mass (Liturgy of the Word, Liturgy of the Eucharist). Confirm reference.
Mane Nobiscum Domine, apostolic letter of John Paul II for the Year of the Eucharist, 7 October 2004. Confirm.
Greek κλάσις τοῦ ἄρτου (Acts 2:42; Luke 24:35 has the dative ἐν τῇ κλάσει τοῦ ἄρτου). Confirm spelling and transliteration.
